lines.title: Intro
lines.text: Hey, I'm Taylor. I'm a real human.

lines.title: Intro
lines.text: I'm also a user experience and product designer, and I'd like to show you something I've been working on.

lines.title: Intro
lines.text: It's called Color Taylor.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: I've always been interested in, but struggled with, how red, green, and blue are used to make the colors on a display.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: Hue, saturation, and brightness, and hue, saturation, and lightness are two approaches that make more sense to me, from working with color wheels for traditional art and design.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: Our focus for this presentation will be HSB.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: Color Taylor is meant to be a playground and educational tool for how RGB and HSB work together.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: You see the relationships in real time, to help better understand how colors work on your display.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: I'll just move myself out of the way.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: The color editor on the right should be familiar to most people who have worked with creative tools.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: The hexagon on the left is a different way of displaying the same information.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: Hue is an angle that ranges from 0 to 360 degrees.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: Red is 0... green is 120... and blue is 240.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: The difference is that red, green, and blue each get their own direction on the hex, matching where they sit on the hue wheel.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: And in between each of these we see combinations: yellow, cyan, and magenta.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: Not to be confused with CMYK, which works differently and is for another time.

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: Let's take an orange as a reference point, 30 degrees.

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: When the hue is set to 30 degrees, I know that's going to be orange, because it's between red and yellow, and yellow is between red and green.

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: So it's a combination of 2 parts red, 1 part green, 0 parts blue.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Adding saturation increases the distance between red, green, and blue.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Desaturating reduces the distance proportionally between these.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Saturation works off the highest value. Red holds still, and green and blue move toward it or away from it.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: When all three are equal, there's no saturation, and you're left with gray.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Notice the hue didn't change, we're still at 30, which is orange. Same hue, only the distance between RGB values changed.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: Brightness is determined by the highest color value.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: As we scale the brightness, the hue and saturation are maintained by scaling the RGB values proportionately to each other.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: Brightness works off zero. All three channels scale together, so the ratios between them stay the same.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: At a hundred percent brightness the hex is at its largest,

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: and lowering it shrinks the size of the hex.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: Notice we stay at the hue 30 orange while moving brightness.

lines.title: Six tints
lines.text: We'll use the swatches section to show how we can use HSB to set six different tints of the same hue.

lines.title: Six tints
lines.text: We can use HSB to come up with a bright desaturated orange, then go down the scale until we have a darker one.

lines.title: Six tints
lines.text: This is really hinting at what a design system does.

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: We've been exploring the playground, but if you want the classroom perspective, check out the equations section.

lines.title: Handoff to the demo
lines.text: Now we can move on to the demo, which gives you an outline of some of the things to look for in the Color Taylor app.

lines.title: Handoff to the demo
lines.text: You can find this demo the first time loading the app,

lines.title: Handoff to the demo
lines.text: or from the question mark button at the top of the app.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Start with the sliders and controls you already know.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Moving one slider will highlight every other slider it affects.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Click the droplet button to switch between Source or Mixed colored sliders.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Click the tags button to show HTML colors on the hex.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Drag a handle on the hex and watch the RGB and HSB sliders follow.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Having fun is the goal of the tool.

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: If you use Figma, I've also made a Color Taylor plugin that you might like to check out.

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: That's Color Taylor!

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: Go play with it, and I hope it helps you see the relationship between RGB and HSB in a different light.

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: If it's useful, I'd like to hear from you. Questions and feedback are welcome.

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: Thanks, see ya.
